narrative: The model estimated your probability of bad credit at 45.0%, meaning that among applicants with a similar profile, roughly 45 in 100 would be expected to have repayment difficulties. The bank treated that level of risk as too high, so your application was denied. The strongest influence on this decision was your credit history. Your record shows no credits or all paid; only about 1% of approved applicants have that same pattern, so it was the most important warning signal and pushed the prediction toward bad credit. The second strongest factor was the status of your checking account. You have a balance in the 0–200 DM range, while most approved applicants had no checking-account information recorded; a low positive balance suggested limited financial cushion and also pushed toward bad credit. By contrast, the requested 12-month term worked in your favour: it is shorter than the approved average of about 19 months, and this factor pushed toward good credit, but it was not enough to offset the first two concerns. To improve your chances, ask the lender for the specific policy reasons, check your credit report for errors, and work on building a clearer recent credit record—for example by making small, regular payments on time and keeping more money in your checking account. Reapplying after those records improve, or with a suitable guarantor, may help.
